channel.title: The Dayly Guide
channel.description: Practical, evidence-aware writing on family organisation, responsibility and children's independence.

item.title: How to reduce the mental load
item.description: Mental load is not the number of tasks you do. It is how much of family life you are continually keeping track of — and that is what has to change.

item.title: How to help children build good study habits
item.description: Retrieval and spacing beat rereading and highlighting, and the habit is far easier to build before exams matter. What to teach, and what to stop doing.

item.title: Stop doing everything on holiday
item.description: The work has not disappeared. It has simply moved somewhere warmer. How to hand real parts of a family holiday to the children who are already there.

item.title: School morning routines that actually work
item.description: Work backwards from the leaving time, move what you can to the evening, and replace your voice with something the child can look at themselves.

item.title: The teen independence checklist
item.description: Work backwards from the day they leave. Six lists covering the house, money, health, travel, deadlines and the personal things nobody writes down.

item.title: Family travel documents checklist
item.description: What to check eight weeks out and two weeks out, the passport-validity rules that catch families out, and what children can carry themselves.

item.title: Beach holiday packing list for families
item.description: Pack less than you think, except for swimwear and sun protection. What to buy when you arrive, and the beach bag a child can own themselves.

item.title: How to teach children to keep track of their belongings
item.description: Children keep track of their things when the environment makes it possible. Fewer things, a clear home for each, and a search the child runs themselves.

item.title: Ski holiday packing list for families
item.description: Everything for the mountain and the resort, what to hire rather than buy for growing children, and the part of the packing children can own themselves.

item.title: How to teach children to break big tasks into steps
item.description: "Clean your room" is not one job. Why children stall on tasks they can do, and how to help them find a first step small enough to start.

item.title: What should children pack themselves? A guide by age
item.description: What a child can pack at two, at eight and at fifteen — and what stays on the adult list at every age, because some things should not be a learning exercise.

item.title: How to help a messy child become more organised
item.description: Mess is usually a storage problem, not a character problem. Fix where things live before you try to change the child.

item.title: Family travel organisation: how to make the holiday belong to everyone
item.description: A timeline from eight weeks out to the morning of departure, a packing system per person, and the parts children should be doing themselves.

item.title: How to stop homework becoming a nightly battle
item.description: Work out what the argument is actually about, then make the task smaller. Five reasons a child resists homework, and what each one needs instead.

item.title: Teaching children about consequences
item.description: Consequences are not punishments. They are what happens when something happens — and removing every one of them removes the information a child learns from.

item.title: The mental load checklist
item.description: A printable list of the invisible work of running a family, by area. Go through it separately, compare, and find out what only one of you was tracking.

item.title: How to teach children to think ahead
item.description: Most morning problems began the evening before. How to move the noticing from the parent to the child, one step at a time.

item.title: How to stop doing everything for your child
item.description: It does not happen through one big decision, but through hundreds of small ones. How to hand responsibility back in stages, without a standoff.

item.title: Family chore systems that survive real life
item.description: The best system is not the fairest on paper. It is the one still running in November, when everyone is tired and nobody is thinking about it.

item.title: Should children be paid for chores?
item.description: Two lessons get confused here. What the research on rewards actually shows, and why contribution, paid work and pocket money can all exist separately.

item.title: Do reward charts work?
item.description: Sticker charts work briefly and then stop. Here is why, what the research on rewards actually shows, and what to use instead.

item.title: Retrieval practice: the study technique parents should know about
item.description: Rereading creates the feeling of knowing. Closing the book and trying to remember is what actually builds it — and it takes a few minutes at a time.

item.title: How to stop reminding your child about everything
item.description: Reminders feel like help and function like a subscription. A staged plan for replacing your voice with something a child can check themselves.

item.title: What is the mental load?
item.description: The invisible work of noticing, remembering and deciding for a household — what it is, why it lands on one person, and what actually shifts it.

item.title: The 10-minute homework rule: what it actually means
item.description: Ten minutes per school year is a rule of thumb, not a finding. Use it as a ceiling rather than a target — and tell the teacher when the work overruns it.

item.title: Chores are not the same as responsibility
item.description: A chore is a task you are told to do. A responsibility includes noticing it needs doing. Only one of them makes you unnecessary.

item.title: How to teach children time management
item.description: Children are poor at estimating time because nobody teaches them. Three skills, in order, and the exercises that build each one.

item.title: Age-appropriate responsibilities, from 3 to 17
item.description: What children can realistically own at each age — personal, household and organisational — with the signal that tells you they are ready for the next thing.

item.title: How to make chores less of a battle
item.description: Before deciding a child is lazy, look at the job. Vague instructions, reminders that became the system, and standards nobody agreed on explain most of it.

item.title: How to teach children responsibility
item.description: Responsibility is not a trait you wait for. It is built by owning real things with real consequences — here is how to hand them over, age by age.

item.title: How to help with homework without doing it for them
item.description: Own the conditions, not the work. The line between supporting homework and taking responsibility for it, and what to say when a child is stuck.

item.title: How to teach children to organise themselves
item.description: Children are not disorganised on purpose. They are missing external structure. Here is how to build it, hand it over, and remove yourself from it.

item.title: Age-appropriate chores, from 3 to 17
item.description: A realistic list of household jobs by age, what to expect at each stage, and how to tell when a child is ready for more.

item.title: How to get kids to help around the house
item.description: Why children resist household jobs, what the research on motivation actually supports, and a system that survives a busy term.

item.title: How to organise multiple children’s schedules
item.description: Three children, two schools, five clubs and one car. How to build a week that works and spot the clashes before they happen.

item.title: Why homework doesn’t work — and how it could
item.description: The research says homework does little for primary pupils. The more useful question is why — and what a version that worked would actually look like.

item.title: How to create family routines that hold
item.description: Routines reduce decisions, arguments and mental load — but only if they are short, triggered by events rather than clocks, and survive a bad week.

item.title: How to organise school life
item.description: School generates more family logistics than anything else. A system for capturing it once, keeping it in one place, and handing most of it to the children.

item.title: How to help children become more independent
item.description: Independence is built by transferring real responsibility in stages, tolerating a worse outcome, and letting small failures land. A practical framework, by age.
